The weather then was much the same as it was today, low‑angled sunlight through patchy cloud lighting up the yellowing birch leaves and bronzing moors on the north-eastern slopes of Kinder Scout. It had picked out the spread wings of a buzzard a little below my eyeline, along with a haze of large insects, which in fact, I quickly realised, were house martins. Such fecundity was thrilling to see, especially as dwindling numbers have put house martins on the red list of threatened species. Dozens swooped and turned just in front of me, and as I looked through this cloud of acrobatic mayhem, dozens more were doing the same in the middle distance, gorging on insects before the long flight south. Today, though, they were gone, the sky empty save for a kestrel quartering her patch, head dropped between her shoulders like a jeweller over her loupe. I wondered where these brave little travellers were now and how many would survive to return. The mere fact of such migrations is astounding, made more so by the mystery that still surrounds them. These birds will winter somewhere in sub-Saharan Africa, but exactly where is unknown.

/science/2026/nov/02/tender-bond-male-do.headline: I saw pedestrians swear at plovers when they swooped. But I admired the birds
/science/2026/nov/02/tender-bond-male-do.excerpt: It was early September when the two spur-winged plover chicks hatched. They hit the ground running, literally. Shortly after emerging from the speckled brown eggs their mother had laid in a shallow divot, they were scurrying around on their disproportionately long, stilt-like legs. They looked like fluffy brown and white cotton balls that could blow away in the wind. The nesting ground was on the headland above a popular tidal pool in Maroubra, in Sydney’s south-east. Adorned with black crowns and bright yellow masks on either side of their bright yellow beak, the chicks’ parents were always close by – and always on guard. They provided protection from the cold, letting their free-roaming chicks tuck themselves under their fluffy white breasts for warmth. And, like all good plover parents, they took turns swooping any intruder – person, dog or drone – who ignored their warning call and came too close – a loud “kekekekekekekek”. A few times I thought I was watching the family from a safe distance only to find myself having to quickly duck to avoid their grey-brown wings clipping my ears. Plovers, otherwise known as masked lapwings, are common throughout northern, central and eastern Australia. These long-legged birds resembling masked superheroes typically inhabit mudflats, marshes, beaches and grasslands – but they’re often seen in urban areas too.

/science/2026/nov/02/tender-bond-male-do.headline: They’re the sopranos of the forest, so what’s silencing the gibbons’ morning chorus?
/science/2026/nov/02/tender-bond-male-do.excerpt: Dawn has broken, and the air is cool and still. It’s at about this time that gibbons usually erupt into song, wa-oo-ing and wa-ing from the highest branches and filling the tree tops with rich melodies. But in this corner of Malaysian forest, bordered by housing and roads, the resident white-handed gibbons are quiet. All that can be heard is the hum of traffic from a nearby highway. This isn’t a rare occurrence for this group of gibbons, according to research, which found these particular gibbons, named Mambang and Walinong, appeared to be producing far fewer morning songs than others that are not exposed to the same level of traffic noise. White-handed gibbons, arboreal animals whose calls can travel more than half a mile through dense forest canopies, are known for their complex songs and vocal techniques that have been likened to those of soprano singers. But as their habitats are increasingly fragmented by roads, industry and urban development, researchers say there is a growing need to understand how human-generated noise is affecting when and how they sing. “Their songs are not just background noise or a way of announcing their presence. They play an important role in communication between groups, territorial interactions and social relationships,” says Nadine Ruppert, associate professor at Xishuangbanna Tropical Botanical Garden, Chinese Academy of Sciences, and a supervisor of the research.

/science/2026/nov/02/tender-bond-male-do.headline: Dogs blink more often when they see owners blinking, study finds
/science/2026/nov/02/tender-bond-male-do.excerpt: Stare into a dog’s eyes and you may encounter a bemused expression. But researchers have found that dogs blink more often when they see their owners doing so, suggesting there may be more to the mutual gaze than meets the eye. Scientists have previously found that dogs turn on the puppy eyes when humans look at them, and that their brains can distinguish happy human faces from other expressions – even telling apart fearful faces from those that are angry or sad. But while previous work has suggested dogs and humans may synchronise their blinking, and dogs may blink more when interacting with their owners rather than a familiar trainer, questions have remained over whether human blinking affects how often dogs bat their eyelids. Dr Chiara Canori, the first author of the new study, from the University of Parma, said: “What we wanted to do here was experimentally isolate the human blink and separate it from all the other things that normally happen during a real social interaction, which has never been done before.” Writing in the journal Royal Society Open Science, Canori and colleagues report how they analysed recordings of 35 dogs of different breeds as each was shown two types of video. Both videos lasted 40 seconds and showed three people, one at a time: the dog’s owner and two unfamiliar humans. In one video, the humans each blinked once every three seconds, and in the other video they looked straight ahead without blinking.
/science/2026/nov/02/tender-bond-male-do.trail: Scientists say research suggests blinking may have acquired a social relevance in interactions between dogs and people
